item.content:encoded:
Miro Kepinski is a film composer and pianist known for crafting emotionally immersive music that blends cinematic intensity with intimate melodic detail. He composed the scores for the Netflix global Top 10 feature Furioza and its midquel Inside Furioza, as well as Netflix’s Lesson Plan, produced by Lightcraft, the studio behind Wonderland starring Mads Mikkelsen.

His work has earned him a nomination for the Hollywood Music in Media Awards and three Fryderyk nominations, recognizing his ability to create music that resonates both on screen and beyond. Alongside his cinematic projects, Miro develops a distinctive neoclassical piano voice, releasing solo works that combine gentle arpeggios, haunting melodies, and atmospheric textures.

Whether scoring films, documentaries, or crafting solo piano pieces, Miro’s music is defined by its narrative depth, emotional clarity, and cinematic scope, offering listeners a journey that is both intimate and grand.

Today, we are happy and proud to be in conversation with Miro, delving into his music path so far and exploring his recent release “Whispers Between the Stars,” alongside his other projects.

1. Dear Miro, welcome to Modern Classical Music Magazine. Could you briefly introduce yourself to our readers and share something that summarizes your musical vision?

It’s great to be here—thank you for the invite. I’m a composer who started this journey out of pure passion, and I’ve been continuing it ever since. Over the years, I’ve explored a wide range of genres—from metal and rock to jazz, classical, and electronic—constantly searching for my own musical language and defining my style.

Where I am now, working as a film composer, allows me to draw from that full palette while focusing on blending emotion with a cinematic feel.

2. Among your most recent records is “Whispers Between the Stars,” released on April 30th, 2026. From both the title and the music, we can perceive a dense, melancholic, yet hopeful tone. What inspired this piece, and what place does it hold in your musical journey?

The inspiration definitely came from space. The universe is incredibly intriguing and mesmerizing—it really shows its vastness and how small we are in comparison. My track tries to capture that feeling in its tone. Adding post-rock, ambient guitars brings me back to my beginnings, when I used to play that kind of music and would tour across Europe on my own, as a lonely ‘star’. I love to compose and play melancholic music—I think it holds so many emotions and deep feelings that the audience can connect with right away.

3. I believe that music creation is never an isolated event. While “Whispers Between the Stars” has its own meaning, does it also belong to a larger picture within your music path?

Of course, it’s the beginning of relaunching my live career. I do play shows, but I really miss going on tours. This time, I want to perform my own music on my own terms. I also have a lot of composed scores that would be a great addition to my setlist—like the Furioza soundtrack.

As for releases, this track and my previous one, “Falling Quietly in the Rain,” are part of a larger album coming later this year, dedicated to nature and its awesomeness.

4. Your work clearly spans several artistic fields, from feature films, TV series, and documentaries to digital releases and beyond. How do you experience being involved in so many areas? Is it more exciting or exhausting?

It’s definitely more exciting. As I mentioned, I’ve played across many genres in different bands, and now, being a film composer brings that variety back again. I love it. One score can be minimal and classical, like for ‘In This Gray Place’, while another leans more into electronic and post-rock elements, like ‘Furioza’. There are also moments where I explore different directions, like the spaghetti western influences in my soundtrack for ‘Prosta Sprawa’, a TV series.

Right now, I’m working on a film with an electronic underscore, and it’s great to experiment and play around with that sound.

5. You’ve had a significant career in film composition so far. Are there any insights from your previous work you’d like to share with our readers?

Composing for a movie is all about emotions—you’re there to support them. Of course, there are different approaches: you can play against what’s on screen to shift or even “cheat” the viewer, or you can lean in and amplify the feeling of a scene right away. But in the end, it’s always about what serves the film best, keeping your ego low.

6. What about upcoming collaborations, live performances, or shortcoming projects you can tell us about? We’d love to hear what’s next.

Apart from my solo music, I have a few different projects in development. My duo KĘPIŃSKI KOWALONEK is moving toward the next album. I also mentioned the film I’m currently working on, and I’ll be starting a bigger project quite soon—though I can’t share details yet.

When it comes to live shows, I’m preparing for a few bigger concerts. One will be this summer, focused on Polish film music with my friend Hania Derej, and another later this year, also centered around film-oriented music. The rest is in the works.

item.dc:creator: Davide Fasiello

The post Peter Manning Robinson – “Bent Out of Shape” first appeared on Modern Classical Music.
item.content:encoded:
With “Bent Out of Shape,” Peter Manning Robinson offers a first glimpse into Excursions, his upcoming return to solo acoustic piano after years of experimentation with his self-invented Refractor Piano™.

The track immediately signals a shift in approach. Where Robinson’s recent work has focused on expanding the instrument’s sonic possibilities, “Bent Out of Shape” feels grounded and direct—built on touch, phrasing, and a sense of movement that leans toward release rather than tension. There is a lightness to the piece, carried by playful rhythmic gestures and gently shifting harmonies, that suggests a conscious move toward clarity.

That sense of lift is not superficial. Written in response to a period of personal and global strain, the piece reads as a search for balance rather than a simple expression of joy. The melodic material unfolds with a natural, almost conversational flow, avoiding both excessive ornamentation and overt dramatics. Robinson resists the temptation to overstate, allowing space and pacing to shape the emotional impact.

What stands out is the control behind the apparent spontaneity. His background in both classical composition and jazz improvisation is evident in the way ideas evolve—subtly, without sharp transitions, giving the piece a feeling of continuity rather than contrast. It’s a restrained approach, but one that reinforces the track’s underlying intent.

As a preview of Excursions, “Bent Out of Shape” suggests a project rooted less in innovation and more in introspection. If Robinson’s recent work has been about redefining the piano, this upcoming release appears to be about reconnecting with it.

The result is a single that doesn’t aim to overwhelm, but to realign—quietly, and with intention.

item.title: Between Keys and Circuits: Michael Keane’s Meditative Debut
item.dc:creator: Davide Fasiello
item.description:

The post Between Keys and Circuits: Michael Keane’s Meditative Debut first appeared on Modern Classical Music.
item.content:encoded:
Life Science Records, 2026

In an increasingly saturated landscape of modern classical crossover, Michael Keane’s debut under his own name stands out less for radical innovation and more for the clarity of its artistic intent.

Titles Electronica is built on a deceptively simple premise: reworking contemporary piano compositions through an electronic lens, reshaping them into something more expansive and textural. The result is a record that moves fluidly between intimacy and abstraction, maintaining a careful balance between acoustic performance and digital manipulation.

The opening track, “Little One,” sets a restrained and fragile tone, functioning more as an invitation than a statement. It’s within the multi-part “Absent Spectator” sequence, however, that Keane’s voice fully emerges. Originating from an improvised session, the material is deconstructed and reassembled across several iterations, each version exploring a different emotional and sonic dimension. Rather than treating these as remixes, Keane approaches them as evolving studies—variations that deepen the core idea instead of simply diversifying it.

This modular approach becomes one of the album’s defining strengths. Instead of constantly introducing new themes, Keane focuses on transformation and nuance, allowing subtle shifts in texture and atmosphere to carry the narrative forward. The electronic elements never overpower the piano; they expand its spatial and emotional reach, creating environments rather than foreground gestures.

Comparisons to artists such as Nils Frahm, Philip Glass, and Jon Hopkins are inevitable, particularly in the interplay between repetition, minimalism, and cinematic ambience. Yet Keane’s background in electronic production—under various aliases—adds a distinct sensibility. There is a clear attention to sound design, with synthesizers used not as decoration but as structural components that shape the listening experience.

Tracks like “Little One Mirage” and “Fever Dream” push further into ambient territory, emphasizing mood over momentum. These moments highlight Keane’s ability to sustain tension without relying on overt melodic development, favoring gradual immersion instead.

That said, the album’s commitment to restraint occasionally works against it. The persistent focus on subtle variation can blur the overall dynamic arc, and listeners seeking sharper contrasts or more pronounced evolution may find parts of the record overly uniform. Still, this feels like a deliberate aesthetic choice rather than a shortcoming.

As a debut under his own name, Titles Electronica presents a cohesive and thoughtfully constructed body of work. It doesn’t attempt to redefine the genre, but it demonstrates a strong sense of direction and a refined understanding of how piano and electronics can coexist. More importantly, it suggests a composer with a clear trajectory—one that could naturally extend into film and visual media.

The post Presenting Luca Basile’s new Album “Verso Casa” — where home becomes a feeling, rather than a place first appeared on Modern Classical Music.
item.content:encoded:
Luca Basile is an eclectic cellist and music composer whose creations range from electronics to classical, with influences from rock and metal. Originally from Taranto, Basile studied cello at the Tito Schipa conservatory, in Lecce. Soon after, he continued researching and experimenting, in close company with his cello. Thanks to his determination and passion, Luca toured in China, the UK, the United Arab Emirates, Serbia, Ukraine, the Netherlands, Belgium, and Latvia. His effort additionally includes works with orchestras, bands, duos, and soloists, which led to the release of several recordings. Basile defines his path forward as stages of a journey, still in motion and evolution, and we are extremely happy to present a review of his recently released Album “Verso Casa.”

Luca Basile – “Verso Casa”

After “Il Viaggio” (2023), Luca Basile now returns with “Verso Casa,” an album whose main goal is to explore a return to the interior: a journey through the innerself, in which “home” is not a synonym for a physical place, but rather for an emotional state, in which to find oneself.

The Album is carefully built around Basile’s main voice: the cello. In the record, in fact, the instrument acts as a sort of guiding soul, capable of driving the listeners’ experience towards several phases of thought and, in a sense, of life.

Musically speaking, the Album blends elements of cinematic pop, electronic, and rock, generating sonic phrases and evolutions that alternate strength and introspection, energy and stillness. Through the different tracks, we can perceive Basile’s identity, which we would gently define as an on-point balance between an impetuous wave and a slow-paced breath.

As the album-opener track, we have the homonymous “Verso Casa,” written together with Lino Pariota, which is a statement of Basile’s ability to create pleasant and engaging musical phrasings. As we move forward, we encounter dramatic and cinematic works such as “Aria,” a masterfully crafted multi-layer in which piano, percussion, and cello speak to each other. As we approach the core of the Album, we discover the tender and fragile “Melodia,” a whispered dialogue to the wind, or to the mirror, who knows.

In Basile’s music, we are set free to both interpret and create our own meanings behind each musical experience. As we slowly move towards the closure, we meet with “Itaca.” Sounding as a second overture, the piece reveals the underlying hope that resides in human beings. The music condensates the feelings of adventure and discovery that are inside all of us, eventually showing how the artists’ work is not only a personal trajectory but rather a universal depiction. The Album ends with “Noha,” a wide, vast, and thought-provoking finale, perhaps leading to the re-discovery of the whole record itself, as an echo that recalls a new opening.

“Verso Casa” is an Album designed to be unfolded piece by piece, to be discovered and from start to finish, as a book that gathers a grand emotional journey. Masterfully working as the meeting point between several musical influences as well as several personal experiences, Basile’s record is a demonstration of how human identity can merge with sonic creativity. “Verso Casa” ultimately shows how, through different paths, yet again, we can meet at the same destination—the one to eventually call home.

The album, released by INRI Classic, is available in all digital stores and in physical format.

The post Presenting Luca Basile’s new Album “Verso Casa” — where home becomes a feeling, rather than a place first appeared on Modern Classical Music.

item.content:encoded:
Review – Field Notes: Solo Piano Vol. 01 by D. Ellsworth

With Field Notes: Solo Piano Vol. 01, Daniel Ellsworth steps away from his roots in indie pop and genre-blending production to deliver something far more intimate and distilled. The result is a neoclassical work that doesn’t aim to overwhelm, but to quietly unfold.

This is an album built on restraint. Rather than leaning into virtuosity or grand compositional arcs, Ellsworth focuses on nuance—subtle harmonic shifts, spacious phrasing, and melodies that feel discovered rather than declared. There’s a sense of patience running through these ten pieces, as if each note has been given time to breathe and settle.

Echoes of Nils Frahm, Ryuichi Sakamoto, and Keith Jarrett can be felt, particularly in the balance between composition and improvisation. Yet Ellsworth avoids imitation; his voice emerges in the way he lets silence become part of the music itself.

Tracks like drift and reverie feel almost like fleeting impressions—musical sketches that hover between memory and presence. Elsewhere, pieces such as becoming and hiraeth carry a deeper emotional undercurrent, though never tipping into excess. Everything remains measured, intentional, and inward-looking.

What’s especially compelling is how Ellsworth’s broader musical background subtly informs the record. Beneath the minimalism lies a songwriter’s instinct for melody and structure, alongside a jazz-influenced openness that keeps the music from feeling rigid. It’s this interplay that gives the album both accessibility and depth.

Field Notes: Solo Piano Vol. 01 is not designed for passive listening. It asks for stillness, for attention, for a willingness to sit with quiet details. In return, it offers a listening experience that feels personal and unguarded—less like a performance, and more like a series of private reflections gently shared.

The post Between Silence and Noise: The Inner Landscapes of “Entre Ruidos” first appeared on Modern Classical Music.
item.content:encoded:
In an era saturated with overstimulation, Entre Ruidos emerges as a quietly insistent work that explores the fragile space between external chaos and inner stillness. Greek composer and pianist Roxani Chatzidimitriou crafts an album that does not merely reference the “noise” of contemporary life, but actively shapes it into a reflective sonic environment.

Blending elements of neoclassical writing, cinematic pacing, and electroacoustic textures, the album resists easy categorization. The instrumentation—piano at its core, surrounded by string quartet, clarinets, double bass, percussion, and electronics—creates a layered and fluid sound world. Rather than foregrounding virtuosity, Chatzidimitriou focuses on atmosphere and emotional continuity, allowing each piece to unfold with a sense of suspended time.

There is a notable sensitivity in the way acoustic and electronic elements coexist. Electronics are never intrusive; instead, they function as an extension of the acoustic palette, subtly expanding the harmonic and spatial dimensions. This approach aligns her work with a broader contemporary classical aesthetic, yet retains a distinct personal voice, occasionally colored by understated references to Greek musical idioms.

What stands out most is the album’s emotional architecture. Moments of tension and density gradually dissolve into passages of introspection, suggesting an internal dialogue rather than a linear narrative. The music often feels like it is hovering “in between”—between movement and stasis, clarity and ambiguity, control and surrender. This liminal quality reflects the conceptual core of the project: the search for authenticity within a world of constant distraction.

While some listeners may find the pacing deliberately restrained, this is precisely where the strength of Entre Ruidos lies. It demands attention, patience, and a willingness to slow down—qualities increasingly rare in both music consumption and daily life.

Following years of compositional development and international recognition, Chatzidimitriou delivers a work that is both cohesive and introspective. Entre Ruidos does not aim to overwhelm; instead, it invites the listener inward, offering a space for contemplation that feels both personal and quietly universal.

The post In Conversation with Francesca Guccione – Panta Rhei (An Ontology of Becoming) first appeared on Modern Classical Music.
item.content:encoded:
Francesca Guccione is an Italian composer and violinist.

Fascinated from the very beginning by the relationship between sound and image, she combined her violin training with studies in composition and film scoring, earning a Master’s degree in this field with highest honors. Her writing moves between chamber music, analog electronics, and studio production, exploring sound as a perceptual architecture of time: ostinatos, cycles, and timbral transformations do not become propulsion, but suspension and immersion.

In 2021 she released her debut modern classical album Muqataea on the French label Whales Records, featuring renowned cellist and composer Giovanni Sollima as artistic director of the project. In 2022 she released the EP Utopia Aerial View, produced in collaboration with Moog Music. In September 2024 she released her second album The Geometry of Time on the Berlin-based label Neue Meister, followed in March 2026 by Panta Rhei: An Ontology of Becoming, also on the same label.

Alongside her discography, she performs widely across Europe in festivals and venues such as Opera Prima Festival, Blaues Rauschen 2025, and Superbooth 25. She has also been hosted at the Colosseum in Berlin—also as an opening act for Hans-Joachim Roedelius—and performed at the National Museum of Warsaw for the event Bal Surrealistyczny.

Today we welcome Francesca to our Magazine with an exclusive interview.

1. Dear Francesca, it’s our pleasure to welcome you to Modern Classical Music Magazine. Could you introduce yourself to our readers and share with us what’s behind your musical vision?

Thank you so much for the invitation. Rather than thinking about my music in strictly stylistic terms, I prefer to imagine it as a meeting point between notation, sound, and perception. What interests me most is the way music can shape our relationship with time, not only as development or direction, but also as suspension, transformation, return, and stratification.
My vision probably comes from a constant tension between different elements that I try to hold together: instrumental gesture and timbral material, the acoustic and electronic dimensions, notation and a more plastic approach to sound. For me, composing does not simply mean organizing notes, but building a sensitive environment in which every detail—a resonance, a timbral shadow, a repetition, a micro-variation—can carry expressive weight. At the same time, beyond the more strictly musical aspect, my relationship with music is deeply connected to introspection and to listening to my own inner world. Composition, for me, is also a way of approaching that which is often difficult to name directly: emotional states, inner movements, and forms of perception that exist before language. In this sense, music becomes a space in which something intimate can take shape and, at the same time, open itself to others.
I believe, and hope, that this inner dimension can find points of resonance with the sensitivity of those who listen to my work. Music is communication, and I feel that the destiny of music—and perhaps of musicians as well—is to try to create spaces for encounter, listening, and shared presence. The most profound and meaningful experiences of my life have always happened through music, or thanks to it, and this inevitably shapes the way I compose and the kind of relationship I seek with those who listen.
I am deeply drawn to music that does not impose itself in a didactic way, but instead leaves space for listening, immersion, and a more subtle form of presence. In this sense, I feel that my artistic work revolves around the possibility of making sound something living and mutable, something one can move through rather than decode in a single, fixed way.

2. Your most recent Album, “Panta Rhei (An Ontology of Becoming),” was released on March 20th, 2026. In it, we find several feelings, dynamically blooming throughout the record: from poignance to pathos. Was there a specific inspiration behind the creation of this work, and what place does it hold in your musical journey?

Yes, I would say that Panta Rhei did not originate from a single, clearly defined inspiration, but rather from a sustained dwelling within a certain idea of transformation. The title clearly evokes the concept of becoming, but for me it was never about translating a philosophical notion into music in an illustrative way. Instead, it was a way of artistically inhabiting a condition that felt very close to me, one in which forms are never entirely stable, emotional states are constantly shifting, and even what seems still is, in fact, already in motion.
The album came into being very organically, not as a project that was rigidly defined from the outset, but as a group of pieces that gradually began to reveal a deep continuity among themselves. At a certain point, I realized that they were all gravitating around the same tension: that between permanence and change, between recurrence and metamorphosis. This is also why the record is shaped by ostinatos, cycles, returns, and timbral transformations that do not simply serve to build form, but to make a process perceptible.
I feel that Panta Rhei represents a central milestone in my journey, as it gathers, in a more mature and conscious way, several lines that have long been part of my artistic research: the relationship between strings and electronics, the attention to time as an inner experience, and the desire to let notation, production, and timbral exploration coexist within a single expressive space.

3. I could witness from your music that the act of creation is never a fragmented circumstance. There is a before, and there will be an after. How is this Album placed in the bigger picture of your discography and of your artistic path forward?

Yes, for me, every work always comes from a before and, inevitably, opens onto an after. I have never experienced an album as an isolated episode, but rather as a stage within a broader process, in which certain questions return, deepen, and change shape. In this sense, Panta Rhei stands in full continuity with my path, while also representing a point of greater awareness.
I feel that it gathers some of the tensions that were already present in my previous works, such as my interest in time, repetition, timbral transformation, and that subtle dialogue between notation and sonic processing. Here, however, these elements feel more integrated, more essential, almost more internalized. There is less distinction between composition, sound, and production, and a greater trust in allowing the music to take shape through gradual processes, transitions, and micro-shifts.
If I look at my discography, I see Panta Rhei as a point of synthesis. Not a detour, but a convergence. It is an album that brings together many trajectories of my research and, at the same time, allows me to sense new possibilities for the future. I am increasingly interested in working in that boundary where instrumental gesture, electronics, the perception of time, and the architecture of sonic space fuse into a singular, unified dimension. At the same time, every record is always a profound work of introspection for me—a way to explore, understand, and bring order to my inner world. For this reason, I feel that the “after” of this album will not be a departure from what I have done so far, but perhaps a way of going even deeper. Rather than changing direction, I feel the desire to continue digging further into a language I am still discovering, seeking ever clearer forms through which to give shape to this relationship between sonic material, transformation, and listening.

4. Your deep interest in the world of art and music clearly encompasses and overcomes several boundaries, making your work a rather multi-field research. How did it all start? Was there a spark or a happening that whispered to you, “music is my way of expression”?

I believe that, at the beginning, there was above all a very instinctive attraction to sound, even before any fully conscious decision. Quite early on, I felt that music was, for me, a natural way of relating to what I could not completely express through words. Not simply as an emotional vehicle, but as a space in which sensation, imagination, and thought could coexist very freely.
As I grew, that initial intuition gradually became more articulated. I realized that what fascinated me was not only the instrumental or performative aspect, but also everything that surrounds sound: its ability to suggest images, to alter the perception of time, to build inner environments, and to enter into dialogue with other artistic forms. I think that is where the more transversal dimension of my work began.
There was not a single revelatory moment, but rather a series of gradual recognitions. Yet, if I try to isolate a memory that profoundly shifted my understanding of what music could do, I think back to when I was very young, playing my violin in Sicily. I was invited to play at a nursing home, and there was an elderly woman who was at the very end of her life, incredibly fragile and fading. Yet, while I was playing, she unexpectedly found the breath and energy to sing an old romantic song for a few brief minutes, with a voice I will never forget. For those few moments, across generations and right on the threshold of her slipping away, we truly met. Experiencing how sound could reach into such a profound, almost inaccessible place—how it could create such a shared presence—left me deeply moved.
Over time, through experiences like this, I understood that music was not only something I studied or practiced, but a real way of thinking, of observing, of giving shape to reality, and also to what remains more invisible within it. Perhaps that is precisely why my path has moved so naturally between composition, violin, electronics, image, and research. I have never felt these fields as separate, but rather as parts of the same expressive and cognitive gesture. And in a certain sense, even my current research begins there: from the desire to understand more deeply how sound can become form, space, and thought.

5. Nowadays, it is getting more and more demanding to both maintain an authentic artistic identity over time, as an artist, and to simultaneously embody a work that pushes us towards continuous deals, industry compromises, and business-related strategies. Above all, we are no longer just composers, but we have to be the managers of ourselves and our salvation. Did this multi-approach shape your working vision?

​I think this condition has above all made more visible a tension that now belongs to the lives of many artists: on the one hand, the need to preserve an authentic core within one’s own artistic research; on the other, the fact that every work is born and moves through networks, contexts, mediations, and concrete structures. Rather than shaping my vision from the outside, this complexity has pushed me to clarify even more carefully what, for me, must
remain essential. At the same time, it is very important to me that this multiplicity of roles does not end up emptying the most authentic core of artistic work. I try to experience everything that surrounds music not as a purely external superstructure, but as something that, when approached consciously, can enter into dialogue with the artistic vision itself. I am thinking, for example, of the way a project is built, how it is narrated, which contexts are chosen, and which collaborations are brought into being. These too are, in part, choices of form. That said, I also consider myself fortunate, because I have not had to carry everything entirely on my own. My husband, for instance, has always helped me greatly and continues to do so, taking care of the visual aspects and other elements related to the broader context of the projects. This matters a great deal to me, because it allows me to feel that the visual dimension also emerges from an authentic dialogue, rather than from a strategy imposed from outside. In the same way, I have been fortunate to collaborate with engineers, professionals, and labels for whom the artistic vision comes first. I am thinking, for example, of Neue Meister, with whom I have always felt a genuine attention to the quality of the project and to its deeper identity.
Perhaps, more than a “multi-approach,” I would speak of a figure that is now inevitably porous, in which composition, production, critical thought, organization, and mediation coexist. In my case, this has certainly shaped my working vision, but it has also led me to seek an even more rigorous balance: to protect the deeper time of creation, while not refusing the concrete reality in which music today takes shape and circulates. I also believe that art, by its very nature, must preserve a zone of independence in relation to the system that receives it, distributes it, or at times conditions it. Not in the naive sense of being able to place itself outside the world, because that is not possible, but in the sense of not allowing the system to exhaust the meaning of the work. For a work of art to remain alive, it must preserve something that exceeds the logic of adaptation, positioning, or function. For me, the center always remains the sound, the quality of the research, and the expressive necessity behind it. Everything else matters, but it must remain in relation to that core, not replace it.

6. Moving towards the future and the upcoming steps forward, are there any relevant projects you would like to highlight and share with us? Upcoming collaborations, planned concerts, or Albums. We would love to hear what is next.

​At the moment, I find myself in a very intense and fertile phase. On the one hand, I am still very much living through the release of Panta Rhei, and it has been deeply meaningful to see the album resonate internationally so soon after its release, across a wide range of Apple Music editorial playlists, featured in the header of Apple Music Classical, and in the Classical charts in Italy and in several other countries. I receive all of this with gratitude, above all because it shows that very personal music can still travel widely and create connection. On the other hand, several other lines of my work are also maturing in parallel. Alongside my activity as a composer, I also pursue an artistic research path that has become increasingly central to me. An important part of the coming period will in fact be connected to my PhD, which I am developing around the relationship between instrumental writing, digital production, spatialization, and new possibilities for notation. It is a path that does not concern theoretical reflection alone, but has a very concrete impact on my compositional practice. The conferences and public moments of exchange I am currently involved in, for example in contexts such as the Royal Birmingham Conservatoire and the IULM University of Milan, are also part of this process, because they represent valuable occasions to share, test, and further refine the directions of my research.
Alongside this, I am working on new performative forms and live installations that are already at a rather advanced stage of development. At the moment, some of the contexts and venues in which these works may be presented are also beginning to take shape. This is something I care about deeply, because for me the live dimension is never a simple transposition of musical material, but a space in which sound can redefine itself through its relationship with environment, presence, and listening. I am also continuing to develop The Sonic Atelier, which is a very important part of my research path and of my reflection on the contemporary composer. Through this project, I have had the opportunity to engage in dialogue with artists such as Caroline Shaw, Volker Bertelmann, Rafiq Bhatia, and Robot Koch, and I would like to continue growing this space as a place for exchange on today’s compositional practices, between writing, production, music for images, performance, and sonic thought. At the same time, I am already working on new music, and the next album is also at a rather advanced stage from a compositional point of view. More generally, I feel that what is coming next does not arise from a desire to change skin artificially, but from the wish to go further and deeper into a language in which sound, space, and transformation can belong to the same expressive breath. There are also some ongoing conversations around possible future developments, including synchronization opportunities and new professional contacts, but what remains essential for me is that every project continues to emerge from a real necessity and from a coherent artistic vision.

The post Listening to What Remains: The Quiet Gravity of Euterpe first appeared on Modern Classical Music.
item.content:encoded:
With Euterpe, Joel D. Hitos delivers a work that naturally sits within the contemporary neoclassical landscape while consciously avoiding being confined by it. More than a simple instrumental album, Euterpe unfolds as an intimate narrative journey built around the idea of inspiration—that elusive presence that appears, guides, and then disappears.

From the opening Euterpe Prelude, the listener is drawn into a sparse, almost ritualistic sonic space where the piano functions not just as an instrument but as an evocative voice. It feels less like a beginning and more like an invocation, immediately establishing the contemplative tone of the entire record.

The emotional core emerges in What Remains and The Deep, where themes of loss and faith are explored without ever slipping into melodrama. Here, Hitos shows a refined sensitivity in his use of time and repetition—hallmarks of minimalism that are employed with clear narrative intent.

One of the album’s most compelling moments comes with the diptych Summer Overture and End of Summer. Brief yet impactful, these pieces capture the fleeting nature of memory. In particular, End of Summer—along with its closing solo piano version—stands out as a highlight, thanks to its essential yet deeply evocative writing.

The album follows a clear arc: All Things New introduces a turning point, a sense of renewal that continues into The Safe Place, where subtle synth textures expand the sonic palette without disrupting its intimacy. This is where one of the project’s central ideas becomes most evident: music as a form of refuge.

Still Remains acts as a mature reflection on earlier themes, translating emotional growth into a more spacious and self-aware compositional approach. The album closes with Come, Euterpe and the solo piano reprise of End of Summer, offering a restrained ending that resists resolution and instead lingers in silence and resonance.

What sets Euterpe apart is its atmospheric coherence paired with a nuanced expressive range. Hitos moves between minimalist piano writing, romantic undertones, and subtle experimental gestures, maintaining a delicate balance between form and emotion.

His background in film is clearly reflected in the music: each piece feels like a scene, each transition like a narrative shift. Yet the album stands firmly on its own, precisely because of its ability to suggest imagery without relying on it.

Euterpe does not aim to impress through technical excess or dense production. Its strength lies in restraint, sincerity, and its ability to create a listening space where the audience can recognize themselves. In a landscape often saturated with similar aesthetics, this work stands out for its authenticity and clarity of vision.

A short but substantial album: rather than telling a story, Euterpe invites us to pause—and listen to what remains.

item.content:encoded:
Review: In holiday clothing, out of the great darkness* by Clarice Jensen

On the cutting edge of contemporary classical music is a talented group of cellist-composers. A partial list includes Hildur Guðnadóttir, the celebrated soundtrack composer (Joker, Sicario: Day of the Soldado, Chernobyl, among others), who is currently performing her newest music, “Where to From,” and Julia Kent, whose latest release is anticipated for spring. Joining these artists is Clarice Jensen. Her highly regarded fourth solo record, In holiday clothing, out of the great darkness (Fat Cat Records, 17 October 2025), solidifies her position in the rich field of composer/performers who channel their creativity through the cello.

Also an accomplished soundtrack composer (No Man of God, Ainu Mosir, and Sin Señas Particulares),  Jensen’s solo work uses loops to build cello voices, all heavily processed by effect pedals, which join, build, and play off each other as the music progresses. Her technique creates an astonishing range of sounds, textures, and effects. The result is both powerful and meditative, and often quite beautiful. 

The 40-minute piece, divided into six sections, with unselfconscious nods to Bach’s cello suites, creates the odd effect of hearing a musical piece, while also experiencing a sense of its composition as Jensen adds layer on layer of loops. The resonant, woody sound of the cello dominates the main voice with offshoots, harmonies, and other sounds added as we can imagine the composer’s inner music forming in her mind.

 In the first section, Jenson creates a kaleidoscope of sound colours with just the wood and wire and her bank of effects and piles of looped versions of herself. Towards the end of the section, high in the register, Jensen conjures the sound of a pipe organ, while a low voice mimics bass pedals. This is the longest, most colourful, and most complex section of the set.

Most Bach-like, almost fugue-like, “From A to B” chases themes around the mix. “1,2” is a slow movement, building a long, frankly lovely melody on top of a looped pulse. Then, “2,1” retreats furthest into the artist’s mind, moving deeper into pure ambient sounds, all again conjured from Jensen’s four strings.

“Part 2” traces a simple tune that is harmonized in more of a nod, perhaps, to Johan Pachelbel (of the famous canon) than to J. S. Bach. The final section, “Unity”,  starts darkly with stabs of colour joined by rhythmic loops creating a tuneful chaos. It settles into a quiet simmer as the piece comes to an end.

The evocative title is a quote from the early twentieth-century German poet Rainer Maria Rilke’s generous and sensitive letters to a young admirer. One of their themes is the need for and the benefit of solitude. Jensen’s title reminds us that this recording is the hard-earned result of the composer alone with her ideas and mirrors her composing technique. Themes are played, looped, then improvised upon. In the composer’s words, “It’s a sort of spectrum between what I call like controlled improvisation and music that’s written from the beginning to the end.”

We hear music in our minds without reference to outside sources. Composers seek to recreate these sound-thoughts, using the materials of their art, here the cello, to share them with the world. In Clarise Jensen’s In holiday clothing, out of the great darkness, not only can we hear the results but also imagine the process that the composer went through as she improvised and looped her way towards it. We can experience the lovely holiday clothes but also glimpse into the darkness where they were sewn.


* The lower-case convention is used in the original title and is a quote from author Rainer Maria Rilke’s “Letters to a Young Poet”.

The post Echoes in the Void: Grief Transfigured in Antonio Di Fonzo’s Silent Sorrow first appeared on Modern Classical Music.
item.content:encoded:
With Silent Sorrow, Antonio Di Fonzo delivers one of the most compelling and mature statements of his artistic journey, establishing a compositional voice that moves fluidly between classical tradition and jazz sensibility.

Released in 2026 on Stradivarius Music Label, the piece originates from a personal experience of loss, yet it avoids any trace of superficial sentimentality. Instead, Di Fonzo crafts a layered musical discourse in which grief is examined with clarity and transformed into a complex, deeply communicative sonic experience.

From the very first measures, the piano emerges as a fully narrative instrument. Intimate, introspective melodic lines unfold in delicate balance with richly articulated, often unpredictable harmonies. These lyrical passages are set against moments of heightened dynamic tension, where expressive energy takes shape through dense, at times almost orchestral writing.

One of the most striking aspects of Silent Sorrow lies in its seamless integration of virtuosity within the musical narrative. Technical challenges never appear as mere display; rather, they are organically embedded in the expressive flow, intensifying the sense of inner conflict that permeates the work. This ability to unite formal control with emotional depth reflects a fully mature compositional awareness.

Harmonically, Di Fonzo reveals a refined and stratified language, where his classical training and jazz influences engage in a natural dialogue. The progressions resist predictability, shaping a constantly evolving sonic fabric marked by expansion and contraction, acceleration and suspension.

Silent Sorrow does not simply evoke pain—it inhabits it. It is precisely within this tension between introspection and momentum that the piece finds its most authentic voice. The personal experience is thus elevated into something universal, becoming a sonic journey that resonates deeply with the listener.

With this composition, Antonio Di Fonzo consolidates his artistic identity, demonstrating a rare ability to merge technique, structure, and emotional depth into a distinctive and recognizable language. Silent Sorrow stands as a significant testament to his expressive maturity and a meaningful contribution to the contemporary piano repertoire.
